opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so it's a big deal for us because it's really the difference between a physics experiment and a technology.

Our first prototypes used superconducting circuits. That was a great platform for proving out the core idea, which is that you can harness the natural stochasticity of physical systems, the thermal noise everyone else spends enormous effort suppressing, and use it directly as a computational resource for probabilistic inference and sampling. But superconducting hardware needs cryogenic cooling, it's expensive, and it's hard to scale and deploy. Nobody's going to put a dilution refrigerator in every data center rack, let alone in a phone.

Moving to standard silicon, using conventional transistors operating at room temperature, means we can ride the entire semiconductor manufacturing ecosystem. Decades and trillions of dollars of investment in fabs, tooling, and process know-how suddenly work for us instead of against us. So the question shifts from "can this work in principle?" to "how fast can we scale it?"

There's also a deeper conceptual point. As transistors shrink, they get noisier. Thermal fluctuations become a bigger and bigger fraction of the signal, and the digital paradigm fights that with more energy, more error correction, and more overhead. We're doing the opposite. We're saying the noise is a feature. Small, low-energy devices that naturally fluctuate are exactly what you want for sampling from complex probability distributions. So being on silicon puts us on the right side of the scaling curve. The further you push into the regime where digital struggles, the better the thermodynamic approach looks.

And practically, if you believe, as I do, that AI is fundamentally about probabilistic reasoning, and that we're going to be energy-constrained in scaling intelligence, then you need hardware that's natively probabilistic and radically more energy efficient. Getting that onto a manufacturable, room-temperature substrate is the step that makes it real. It's what takes this from a lab curiosity to something that could actually reshape the compute landscape.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it's the difference between a theory and a technology. For years, thermodynamic computing lived in papers and in bespoke experimental setups — we were essentially showing that you could harness physical noise and stochastic dynamics to do useful computation, like sampling from a probability distribution or solving a linear system, and that physics would do it for free, so to speak. But the question that always hangs over a new computing paradigm is, can it ride the curve that made classical computing win? And that curve is CMOS. It's the most refined manufacturing process humanity has ever built, trillions of dollars of accumulated engineering, and anything that can't plug into it tends to stay a lab curiosity.

So getting a thermodynamic chip fabricated on a standard silicon process means a few things at once. One, the noise we're exploiting is no longer something we have to engineer artificially — it's the intrinsic thermal fluctuations of the transistors and capacitors, which everyone else spends enormous effort suppressing. We're treating as a resource what the rest of the industry treats as a bug. Two, it means we can scale. The same foundries, the same packaging, the same tooling. You go from a handful of cells on a bench to potentially millions on a die, and the economics start to look like a real accelerator rather than a physics demo. And three, it changes the conversation with people building AI systems, because now you can actually benchmark energy per sample against a GPU instead of arguing from first principles.

The deeper point, I think, is that all of machine learning is fundamentally about probability — sampling, inference, uncertainty — and we've been simulating that probabilistic world on deterministic digital hardware, generating pseudo-randomness with a lot of arithmetic. Putting the physics itself on silicon closes that gap. The hardware becomes native to the mathematics. That's the part that feels like a breakthrough to me, more than any single number.

astra-6.text:
Because it gives us a path from an interesting physical principle to something we can actually manufacture and scale. You can build a thermodynamic computer using exotic devices, but then you also have to solve the problem of building an entirely new hardware ecosystem. Getting it into silicon means we can work with the fabrication infrastructure that already exists.

The conceptual shift is that thermal noise becomes a computational resource. In a conventional digital computer, you spend energy making sure fluctuations don’t corrupt your bits. Here, we want to engineer a system whose fluctuations help it explore possible states, so that its physical evolution performs the sampling we need. That’s particularly interesting for probabilistic models, where generating samples can be a major computational cost.

So the breakthrough isn’t simply that we’ve made another silicon chip. It’s that we have a route to doing this kind of computation in a familiar manufacturing platform. You still have to demonstrate the advantages at scale, including the cost of control and readout, but it makes that prospect much more concrete.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, the significance is that you can potentially use the physics of the device to do the computation, rather than spending energy simulating that physics. In a thermodynamic computer, fluctuations aren’t just noise you’re trying to suppress. They’re part of how the system explores possibilities and produces samples.

Moving that into silicon gives you a route to building it with a mature manufacturing platform and integrating it with conventional electronics. You still need digital control, you need to get data in and out, and you need to scale up the interactions between the components.

So the breakthrough is bringing that physical computing principle into a platform where you can start engineering a practical machine. That doesn’t automatically establish an advantage for every workload. The next question is whether the sampling benefits survive at scale, once you account for the energy and time of the whole system.
